record.paper_title: On the combinatorics of tableaux -- A notebook of open problems
record.original_question: Are there lattices that obey all orders of the Arguesian law but are not linear? Are there such lattices that are finite?

evidence.quote: [Wor2024b, quest. 3.65] Are there lattices that obey all orders of the Arguesian law but are not linear? Are there such lattices that are finite?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A lattice is a partially ordered set $(L,\le)$ in which every pair of elements $x,y\in L$ has a least upper bound $x+y$ (join) and a greatest lower bound $xy$ (meet). A lattice $L$ is called linear (or a linear lattice) if it is isomorphic to a sublattice of the lattice of equivalence relations on some set, ordered by inclusion, in which the meet operation is intersection of relations and the join operation is given by composition (equivalently, the relations involved pairwise permute under composition).

The Arguesian law is the lattice identity, modeled on Desargues' theorem in projective geometry, which asserts that for any elements $a_0,a_1,a_2,b_0,b_1,b_2$ of $L$,
$$ (a_0+b_0)(a_1+b_1)(a_2+b_2) \le a_0\bigl(a_1+(a_2+c_2)(c_0+c_1)\bigr) + b_0\bigl(b_1+(b_2+c_2)(c_0+c_1)\bigr), $$
where $c_i = (a_j+a_k)(b_j+b_k)$ for $\{i,j,k\}=\{0,1,2\}$. There is a chain of higher-order Arguesian identities, indexed by integers $n\ge 1$, of strictly increasing strength (the case $n=1$ being the classical Arguesian law); each higher Arguesian identity is known to hold in every linear lattice.

Say that a lattice $L$ "obeys all orders of the Arguesian law" if $L$ satisfies every Arguesian identity of order $n$ for all $n\ge 1$.

Question: Does there exist a lattice $L$ that obeys all orders of the Arguesian law but is not a linear lattice? If so, does there exist such a lattice $L$ that is finite?
artifact.status_search_result: The chain of higher-order Arguesian identities introduced by Haiman is known to be properly increasing in strength and to hold in all linear lattices, but the converse — whether satisfying all higher Arguesian identities forces linearity — is not resolved in the literature surveyed; recent surveys (2024) and notebooks of open problems list this as an open question, with no finite or infinite counterexample known.

status_evidence.title: A survey of lattice properties: modular, Arguesian, linear, and distributive
status_evidence.snippet: Higher Arguesian identities of increasing strength all hold in linear lattices; the relationship between satisfying them all and linearity is discussed.
status_evidence.claim: The implication from satisfying all higher-order Arguesian identities to linearity is not established.

status_evidence.title: Arguesian lattice - Encyclopedia of Mathematics
status_evidence.snippet: The Arguesian identity is a lattice-theoretic version of Desargues' theorem; linear lattices satisfy the Arguesian law and its strengthenings.
status_evidence.claim: Linear lattices form a proper subclass of Arguesian lattices, with no known finite separating example for the full chain.
